title: Ealasaid nic Iain's lamp goes dark
summary: Ealasaid nic Iain, who alone had kept a lamp burning in the harbour-house window at Seann Skell after the rest of the waterfront let the custom lapse, dies in her own bed, and no one after her sets a light there again.

title: Eòghann mac Nèill keeps the book with the window dark
summary: Eòghann mac Nèill, harbour scribe of Seann Skell, passes the harbour-house window each rite-day and finds no reason offered for a light to be set there again; he enters nothing of it in his own book, which is kept for the number, the weather and the tide alone.

title: Death of Aonghas mac Lachlainn
summary: Aonghas mac Lachlainn dies at Cathair dhearg, four-and-eighty years old, the last of the council that had refused Clann Choinnich's Athchuingean an Airgid; asked once more on his deathbed why he had turned his own vote, he answers only that his reason had not stopped seeming good to him, and says no more.

title: A rider of Muileann chiar attends the burying he was never asked to
summary: A rider sent down by the silver guild of Muileann chiar on the strength of an old courtesy stands at the back of Aonghas mac Lachlainn's small burying at Cathair dhearg, and no one there asks him why a guild his vote had cost a fortune troubled to send anyone at all.

title: Na Seachd Taighean name themselves Comhairle a' Chùraim
summary: Meeting at Cathair dhearg by chance of their riders' errands rather than by any summons, the heads of Na Seachd Taighean call themselves Comhairle a' Chùraim, the council of the custody, and name Tormod mac Ailein, eight-and-thirty years old and a custodian's son of no house among the seven, Ceann a' Chùraim to speak for them with one voice.

title: Clann Choinnich's question is set aside at the first sitting
summary: At the same sitting that names the council of the custody, Clann Choinnich alone asks whether the silver might be raised again; the board sets the question aside mildly, unwilling to test a new council on the one asking that had already cost the last one a member's death.

title: The queen's chair is left standing empty
summary: Na Seachd Taighean leave the chair at the head of the board, the queen's own, standing empty at every sitting after her name is no longer spoken; Tormod mac Ailein, offered it, keeps his place at the board's foot instead, and in time no clerk living can say with certainty whose absence the chair still marks.

title: The council's letters keep no name above the seal
summary: The newly named council of the custody sends out its letters from Cathair dhearg sealed with Taigh na Fèithe's own trellis and hollow stone and no name written above the seal, continuing without comment a custom An Talla Dearg's clerks had already begun in the queen's last silent years.

title: Mànas mac Dhùghaill writes that the mist lies thinner
summary: Mànas mac Dhùghaill, priest of Manannan's rite at Seann Skell, sets down for the first time in his own book a thing the older priests had only ever said at the hearth: that the grey past the headlands stands thinner each year, and that he cannot say whether saying the prayer at every tide holds anything back at all.

title: Oighrig nic Eachainn sees the line of the open sea
summary: A fisher of Ceann mhòr, Oighrig nic Eachainn, rests on her oars past where the rule of sight-of-land strictly allows and sees, for a few breaths before the grey closes again, a hard dark line beyond the mist, ruled clean across the edge of the world.

title: Oighrig keeps what she saw to her own mother
summary: Oighrig nic Eachainn turns for home as the rule says and tells no priest and no reeve what she saw beyond the mist, speaking of it months after only to her own mother, who tells her she has already shown better sense in the keeping of it than most who see such things at all.

title: The last winter of the age
summary: On a still morning near the year's dark heart, the priests of Manannan pray at every tide at Seann Skell, the boats of Ceann mhòr turn for home before the rule strictly asks it of them, and the council keeps its board at Cathair dhearg with the chair at its head still empty, while the harbour-house lamp-window that once marked Oidhche nan Lòchran stands dark for another winter.

title: Eòghann mac Nèill counts the rite of the eleven
summary: At Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh on Cidhe an Diosail, Eòghann mac Nèill, eleven years the quay's scribe, stands back as the scribe's place requires and counts the people on the stones twice, once by eye and once by name: eleven.

title: An Talla Dearg holds five hundred souls
summary: In the year Na Seachd Taighean name their council, An Talla Dearg at Cathair dhearg holds perhaps five hundred souls in all its lanes and closes, fewer than the tenants of a single one of Na Seachd Taighean in a good year.

title: Eòghann mac Nèill at the last winter
summary: Six-and-twenty years the scribe of Cidhe an Diosail, Eòghann mac Nèill walks down to the stones each Là an Diosail with the same board under his arm and writes the number, the weather and the tide in the same plain hand.
